drug_class: Nasal decongestant (alpha-adrenergic agonist); also used as a topical treatment for facial redness
purpose: Oxymetazoline is most commonly used as a nasal spray to relieve a stuffy nose caused by colds, allergies, or sinus congestion. It works very quickly — usually within minutes. A cream form is also available to reduce persistent facial redness in adults with a skin condition called rosacea.
how_it_works: Oxymetazoline works by narrowing the blood vessels in the lining of your nose or skin. When those blood vessels get smaller, swelling and congestion go down, making it easier to breathe. Think of it like squeezing a garden hose — less blood flow means less swelling and redness.
common_side_effects: Temporary burning, stinging, or dryness inside the nose; sneezing; headache; nervousness or trouble sleeping if absorbed in larger amounts. The skin cream may cause mild skin irritation, itching, or flushing in some people.
warnings: Do not use the nasal spray for more than 3 days in a row. Using it longer can cause 'rebound congestion,' meaning your nose gets even more stuffed up when the medicine wears off — and you feel like you need it more and more. Tell your doctor if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, diabetes, or thyroid problems before using this medication. Avoid use in children under 6 unless directed by a doctor. Do not use if you are pregnant without asking your doctor first.
typical_dosing: Nasal spray (adults and children 6+): 2–3 sprays in each nostril every 10–12 hours as needed. Do not use more than twice in 24 hours. Do not use for more than 3 days. Skin cream (Rhofade): Apply a pea-sized amount to the affected areas of the face once daily in the morning. Always follow the instructions on the package or from your doctor.
